ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Columbia University Institutional Review Board.
Participants were 1052 adults residing in the United States who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study.

Food rating and choice tasks (Figure 1) Participants completed a food rating task in which they rated 46 food items along 17 separate attributes: protein content, fat content, carbohydrate content, vitamin content, sodium content, sugar content, gluten content, caloric content, healthiness, tastiness, how tasty others think the food is, fillingness, savoriness, pleasantness of texture, disgustingness, feelings resulting from the food, and familiarity.
table.formatted: Food rating and choice tasks (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) Participants completed a food rating task in which they rated 46 food items along 17 separate attributes: protein content, fat content, carbohydrate content, vitamin content, sodium content, sugar content, gluten content, caloric content, healthiness, tastiness, how tasty others think the food is, fillingness, savoriness, pleasantness of texture, disgustingness, feelings resulting from the food, and familiarity.

table.text: Next, participants completed a food choice task.

In this task, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat "right now," between a reference food (an item the participant had rated neutrally for tastiness and healthiness) and each of the other 45 foods in their stimulus set.
Participants completed the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire-Revised 18; the Cognitive Restraint subscale assessed restrained eating behavior.

"Self-control" can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty or a food that was tasty and not healthy.

Influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors on food choice across individual characteristics Participants were broadly representative of the United States population in terms of individual characteristics, though more highly educated (Lloyd et al; 2020).
table.formatted: Influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors on food choice across individual characteristics Participants were broadly representative of the United States population in terms of individual characteristics, though more highly educated <ref type="bibr">(Lloyd et al;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2020)</ref>.

table.text: Approximately half (51.0%) of participants were female, and the majority (60.2%) aged between 26 and 40 years.

Participants were significantly more likely to choose more savory rather than sweeter foods, consistent with studies showing that protein content is associated with food preferences in humans (32, 33).
table.formatted: Participants were significantly more likely to choose more savory rather than sweeter foods, consistent with studies showing that protein content is associated with food preferences in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33)</ref>.

table.text: Each participant provided a total of 782 ratings (17 ratings for each of the foods in their 46-item set).

Choice Task After all ratings had been provided, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat "right now," between a reference food (randomly selected from items the participant had rated neutrally on both the tastiness and healthiness scale) and each of the other 45 foods in their specific stimulus set.
When making their food choices, participants were asked to imagine snack-sized portions of the presented foods.

Self-control "Self-control" can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as those trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty (Healthiness rating above that of the reference item, and Tastiness rating below that of the reference item) or a food that was tasty and not healthy (Tastiness rating above that of the reference item, and Healthiness rating below that of the reference item).

Participants were individuals who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study between July 2018 and August 2019 1, recruited using a convenience sampling strategy, and paid $7.25 for study completion.
Participants provided informed consent by clicking an icon to continue with the experiment.

Participants completed ratings of images of food on 17 different attributes, prior to completing a Food Choice phase in which they indicated whether they preferred a food that varied, displayed on the right, or a constant Reference food, displayed on the left.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were 1052 adults residing in the United States who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study.

> Food rating and choice tasks (Figure 1) Participants completed a food rating task in which they rated 46 food items along 17 separate attributes: protein content, fat content, carbohydrate content, vitamin content, sodium content, sugar content, gluten content, caloric content, healthiness, tastiness, how tasty others think the food is, fillingness, savoriness, pleasantness of texture, disgustingness, feelings resulting from the food, and familiarity.

> Next, participants completed a food choice task.

> In this task, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat "right now," between a reference food (an item the participant had rated neutrally for tastiness and healthiness) and each of the other 45 foods in their stimulus set.

> Participants completed the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire-Revised 18; the Cognitive Restraint subscale assessed restrained eating behavior.

> "Self-control" can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty or a food that was tasty and not healthy.

> Influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors on food choice across individual characteristics Participants were broadly representative of the United States population in terms of individual characteristics, though more highly educated (Lloyd et al; 2020).

> Approximately half (51.0%) of participants were female, and the majority (60.2%) aged between 26 and 40 years.

> Participants were significantly more likely to choose more savory rather than sweeter foods, consistent with studies showing that protein content is associated with food preferences in humans (32, 33).

> Each participant provided a total of 782 ratings (17 ratings for each of the foods in their 46-item set).

> Choice Task After all ratings had been provided, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat "right now," between a reference food (randomly selected from items the participant had rated neutrally on both the tastiness and healthiness scale) and each of the other 45 foods in their specific stimulus set.

> When making their food choices, participants were asked to imagine snack-sized portions of the presented foods.

> Self-control "Self-control" can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as those trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty (Healthiness rating above that of the reference item, and Tastiness rating below that of the reference item) or a food that was tasty and not healthy (Tastiness rating above that of the reference item, and Healthiness rating below that of the reference item).

> Participants were individuals who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study between July 2018 and August 2019 1, recruited using a convenience sampling strategy, and paid $7.25 for study completion.

> Participants provided informed consent by clicking an icon to continue with the experiment.

> Participants completed ratings of images of food on 17 different attributes, prior to completing a Food Choice phase in which they indicated whether they preferred a food that varied, displayed on the right, or a constant Reference food, displayed on the left.

Ethics approval statement:

> The study was approved by the Columbia University Institutional Review Board.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Careless Responding

6 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

), "Short-scale only" = c("no", "no", "no", "no", "no", "no")), row.names = c(3L,

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study was approved by the Columbia University Institutional Review Board.
live_data_statements: Participants were 1052 adults residing in the United States who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study.

Food rating and choice tasks (Figure 1) Participants completed a food rating task in which they rated 46 food items along 17 separate attributes: protein content, fat content, carbohydrate content, vitamin content, sodium content, sugar content, gluten content, caloric content, healthiness, tastiness, how tasty others think the food is, fillingness, savoriness, pleasantness of texture, disgustingness, feelings resulting from the food, and familiarity.
Next, participants completed a food choice task.

In this task, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat "right now," between a reference food (an item the participant had rated neutrally for tastiness and healthiness) and each of the other 45 foods in their stimulus set.
Participants completed the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire-Revised 18; the Cognitive Restraint subscale assessed restrained eating behavior.

"Self-control" can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty or a food that was tasty and not healthy.

Influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors on food choice across individual characteristics Participants were broadly representative of the United States population in terms of individual characteristics, though more highly educated (Lloyd et al; 2020).
Approximately half (51.0%) of participants were female, and the majority (60.2%) aged between 26 and 40 years.

Participants were significantly more likely to choose more savory rather than sweeter foods, consistent with studies showing that protein content is associated with food preferences in humans (32, 33).
Each participant provided a total of 782 ratings (17 ratings for each of the foods in their 46-item set).

Choice Task After all ratings had been provided, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat "right now," between a reference food (randomly selected from items the participant had rated neutrally on both the tastiness and healthiness scale) and each of the other 45 foods in their specific stimulus set.
When making their food choices, participants were asked to imagine snack-sized portions of the presented foods.

Self-control "Self-control" can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as those trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty (Healthiness rating above that of the reference item, and Tastiness rating below that of the reference item) or a food that was tasty and not healthy (Tastiness rating above that of the reference item, and Healthiness rating below that of the reference item).

Participants were individuals who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study between July 2018 and August 2019 1, recruited using a convenience sampling strategy, and paid $7.25 for study completion.
Participants provided informed consent by clicking an icon to continue with the experiment.

Participants completed ratings of images of food on 17 different attributes, prior to completing a Food Choice phase in which they indicated whether they preferred a food that varied, displayed on the right, or a constant Reference food, displayed on the left.

#### File paths
**26 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `mTURK_July2025.csv` to `mTurk_July2025.csv` (in mTurk_analyses.Rmd); `mTURK_July2025.csv` to `mTurk_July2025.csv` (in mTurk_analyses_supplement.Rmd); `~/Documents/Github/mTurk_July2025.csv` to `mTurk_July2025.csv` (in M1.R); `~/Documents/Github/src/cleanup.R` to `cleanup.R` (in M1.R); `~/Documents/Github/mTurk_July2025.csv` to `mTurk_July2025.csv` (in M2.R); `~/Documents/Github/src/cleanup.R` to `cleanup.R` (in M2.R); `~/Documents/Github/mTurk_July2025.csv` to `mTurk_July2025.csv` (in M3.R); `~/Documents/Github/src/cleanup.R` to `cleanup.R` (in M3.R); `~/Documents/Github/mTurk_July2025.csv` to `mTurk_July2025.csv` (in M4.R); `~/Documents/Github/src/cleanup.R` to `cleanup.R` (in M4.R), and 16 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. **7 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
**2 file names in the code are not the same as in the deposit**, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.

**`setwd()` in the code**
**3 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

**Calls that install packages in the code**
12 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.
**Run by another script**
1 script is run by another script with `source()`, so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

text.text: Daily food decisions accumulate to impact physical health, but making choices consistent with longer-term health goals can prove challenging.
Prior research has focused predominantly on dampening preferences for highly palatable foods, or exerting self-control, as the mechanism for healthier food choices.
Consequently, the range of cognitive strategies for healthy eating, and how they vary with demographic characteristics, remains unclear.
Here, a large US sample (N = 1,052) completed an online food rating and choice task, and demographic and eating behavior questionnaires.
Participants rated foods across 17 dimensions, which were reduced to three underlying core food attributes by factor analysis: Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami (capturing food savoriness).
All attributes influenced food choices.
A multi-attribute drift diffusion model quantified distinct yet latent choice processes, including the deliberation required prior to making a choice.
The influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami on choice varied across the study population.
Women, individuals endorsing higher levels of eating restraint, and individuals with lower BMI selected subjectively healthier foods more frequently.
Making subjectively healthier choices was not dependent only on engaging self-control.
Rather, individuals making subjectively healthier choices perceived subjectively healthier foods as tastier.
In addition, individuals endorsing high levels of eating restraint required less deliberation when making choices, suggesting more automatic decision-making.
These findings suggest multiple routes to making healthier food choices and question the narrative that food tastiness must be sacrificed to support physical health.
Decisions about what to eat are made multiple times a day, every day.
The accumulated effect of these decisions impacts health and well-being in the short and long term.

Making choices consistent with longer-term health goals is challenging, yet poor diet and (failed) attempts to change diet impose a significant physical and mental health burden for individuals and society (e.g., obesity, cardiovascular disease; (1, 2)).
text.formatted: Making choices consistent with longer-term health goals is challenging, yet poor diet and (failed) attempts to change diet impose a significant physical and mental health burden for individuals and society (e.g., obesity, cardiovascular disease; <ref type="bibr">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr">2)</ref>).

text.text: Understanding of the processes guiding food choice is needed for the development of interventions to improve dietary decision making.

Some research has described differences in eating patterns among different demographic groups (3), but little is known about the cognitive processes that underlie individual variation in food choices.

Here, we characterized how valuation and choice construction processes vary across a large, broadly representative, cohort in the United States (4), with particular focus on factors known to influence dietary decisions: age, gender, BMI, and cognitive restraint around eating (5) (6) (7) (8) (9) (10).

text.text: The determinants of eating behavior are complex.
The neural mechanisms that regulate homeostatic energy intake have been well characterized (11, 12).
text.formatted: The neural mechanisms that regulate homeostatic energy intake have been well characterized <ref type="bibr">(11,</ref> <ref type="bibr">12)</ref>.

text.text: However, food intake is not guided by energy needs alone.
Cognitive and computational neuroscience studies have yielded a framework for understanding multi-attribute decision-making (13) (14) (15).
text.formatted: Cognitive and computational neuroscience studies have yielded a framework for understanding multi-attribute decision-making <ref type="bibr">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(15)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, food choices have largely been examined as the consequence of subjective perceptions of how tasty and healthy food items are.

Brain imaging and behavioral data suggest that food options are evaluated along these dimensions prior to combining evaluations into a weighted sum (16) (17) (18), and that the weight applied to a given dimension varies according to individual motivations, values, and states (17, 19).
text.formatted: Brain imaging and behavioral data suggest that food options are evaluated along these dimensions prior to combining evaluations into a weighted sum <ref type="bibr">(16)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(18)</ref>, and that the weight applied to a given dimension varies according to individual motivations, values, and states <ref type="bibr">(17,</ref> <ref type="bibr">19)</ref>.

text.text: Tastiness and healthiness attributes are generally considered orthogonal and potentially in conflict (16, 17, 19, 20), and subjective tastiness generally exerts a greater influence on food choice (16, (21) (22) (23) (24).
text.formatted: Tastiness and healthiness attributes are generally considered orthogonal and potentially in conflict <ref type="bibr">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr">20)</ref>, and subjective tastiness generally exerts a greater influence on food choice <ref type="bibr">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr">(21)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(24)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the selection of subjectively healthier foods is thought to depend on the exertion of effortful self-control, with studies focusing on the ability to suppress the influence of tastiness (16), to boost the influence of subjective healthiness on choice (17, 25), and approaches to changing the balance between the two influences (17, 26, 27).
text.formatted: Therefore, the selection of subjectively healthier foods is thought to depend on the exertion of effortful self-control, with studies focusing on the ability to suppress the influence of tastiness <ref type="bibr">(16)</ref>, to boost the influence of subjective healthiness on choice <ref type="bibr">(17,</ref> <ref type="bibr">25)</ref>, and approaches to changing the balance between the two influences <ref type="bibr">(17,</ref> <ref type="bibr">26,</ref> <ref type="bibr">27)</ref>.

text.text: However, subjective healthiness and tastiness need not be in conflict.

Challenging the notion that subjectively healthier choices are made only when self-control is implemented, some individuals (e.g., individuals with the eating disorder, anorexia nervosa, or those endorsing high levels of cognitive restraint around eating) find subjectively healthier items tastier, reducing the need for self-control in those choices (5, (21) (22) (23) 28).
text.formatted: Challenging the notion that subjectively healthier choices are made only when self-control is implemented, some individuals (e.g., individuals with the eating disorder, anorexia nervosa, or those endorsing high levels of cognitive restraint around eating) find subjectively healthier items tastier, reducing the need for self-control in those choices <ref type="bibr">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr">(21)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28)</ref>.

text.text: Current understanding of food decisions is also limited by the fact that prior research has focused on the healthiness-tastiness dichotomy, to the exclusion of other attributes that may contribute to the choice process.

We previously found that, in addition to subjective healthiness and tastiness factors, foods varied along a dimension that captured protein content, sodium content, low sugar content, and savoriness (henceforth labelled Umami; (4)).
Studies with animal models indicate that protein appetite drives behavior and is associated with selective reward responses (29) (30) (31).
text.formatted: Studies with animal models indicate that protein appetite drives behavior and is associated with selective reward responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref>.

text.text: A few studies in humans have shown that protein content is associated with food choices (32, 33) and that individuals differ in their liking for sweet versus savory foods (34) (35) (36).
text.formatted: A few studies in humans have shown that protein content is associated with food choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33)</ref> and that individuals differ in their liking for sweet versus savory foods <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(34)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(35)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(36)</ref>.

text.text: How the Umami dimension influences choice in the context of the more commonly studied subjective tastiness and healthiness attributes remains unclear.
Here we examined how subjectively healthy food choices are made, which strategies or combination of strategies are implemented, and by whom.

We characterized the role of Umami as well as Tastiness and Healthiness factors in food choice, examined multiple decision strategies that may promote subjectively healthier choices, and characterized individual differences in food choice (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: We characterized the role of Umami as well as Tastiness and Healthiness factors in food choice, examined multiple decision strategies that may promote subjectively healthier choices, and characterized individual differences in food choice (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: For more granular insight into how food choices are made, we applied computational models (drift diffusion models; DDMs) to choice and rating data to separate and quantify distinct choice processes (e.g., choice caution vs. speed of evidence accumulation for separate attributes).

Analyses revealed that there were multiple paths to making subjectively healthy choices, and that their use varied with individual characteristics (age, gender, BMI, self-reported cognitive eating restraint).
These results have implications for targeted health interventions.
The study was approved by the Columbia University Institutional Review Board.
Participants were 1052 adults residing in the United States who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study.

Food rating and choice tasks (Figure 1) Participants completed a food rating task in which they rated 46 food items along 17 separate attributes: protein content, fat content, carbohydrate content, vitamin content, sodium content, sugar content, gluten content, caloric content, healthiness, tastiness, how tasty others think the food is, fillingness, savoriness, pleasantness of texture, disgustingness, feelings resulting from the food, and familiarity.
text.formatted: Food rating and choice tasks (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) Participants completed a food rating task in which they rated 46 food items along 17 separate attributes: protein content, fat content, carbohydrate content, vitamin content, sodium content, sugar content, gluten content, caloric content, healthiness, tastiness, how tasty others think the food is, fillingness, savoriness, pleasantness of texture, disgustingness, feelings resulting from the food, and familiarity.

text.text: Next, participants completed a food choice task.

In this task, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat "right now," between a reference food (an item the participant had rated neutrally for tastiness and healthiness) and each of the other 45 foods in their stimulus set.
Participants completed the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire-Revised 18; the Cognitive Restraint subscale assessed restrained eating behavior.

Participants' age, gender, height, and weight were obtained by questionnaire. to completing a Food Choice phase in which they indicated whether they preferred a food that varied, displayed on the right, or a constant Reference food, displayed on the left.
The Reference food was selected per individual to be neutral per their ratings of Tastiness and Healthiness.
A factor analysis of ratings yielded three central dimensions, subsequently used to examine food choices and their variation with individual characteristics.
The Tastiness factor captured texture and familiarity, in addition to how tasty a food was rated.
The Healthiness factor captured ratings across various macronutrients in addition to caloric content.
The Umami factor captured a savory/sweet dimension including protein and how filling a food was reported to be.
Analyses were completed in R. For all analysis code, see: https://github.com/CaitlinLloyd/ThoughtForFood.
text.formatted: Analyses were completed in R. For all analysis code, see: <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/CaitlinLloyd/ThoughtForFood">https://github.com/CaitlinLloyd/ThoughtForFood</ref>.

text.text: As described previously (4), an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) applied to the rating data indicated that the 17 ratings were best captured by three factors: a Tastiness factor, a Healthiness factor, and an Umami factor capturing a savory/sweet dimension.
Capitalization of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami will be used to indicate referral to the composite variable.
Logistic mixed effects regression estimated the main effects of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors on choice.

Logistic mixed effects regression examined the interaction between the influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors and individual characteristics of interest (Age, BMI, Gender, Cognitive Restraint).

Mixed effects regression also estimated the main effects of Healthiness and Umami on Tastiness across all participants, and interactions between individual characteristics and the influence of Healthiness and Umami on Tastiness ratings.

The proportion of subjectively healthy choices was calculated as the proportion of trials in which the participant selected the item rated as healthier; multiple linear regression estimated the association with each individual characteristic of interest.

"Self-control" can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty or a food that was tasty and not healthy.
Successful self-control trials were defined as conflict trials in which participants selected the healthy and not-tasty food or did not select the tasty and not-healthy food.

Self-control success was calculated for each participant by dividing the total number of successful self-control trials by the total number of conflict trials; multiple linear regression estimated the association with individual characteristics of interest (covarying for total number of conflict trials).

To assess whether the use of self-control may be less effortful for certain individuals, mixed effects linear regression was used to estimate the difference in response time between successful and unsuccessful self-control trials.

To examine how subjectively healthy choices related to self-control and Healthiness-Tastiness alignment, the proportion of subjectively healthy choices was regressed onto self-control success and Healthiness-Tastiness alignment (extracted from the model estimating the Influence of Healthiness and Umami on Tastiness, described above).
To further elucidate the cognitive mechanisms underlying food choices, several variants of the multi-attribute drift diffusion model (DDM) were implemented (25, 27, 53, 54; Figure 2).
text.formatted: To further elucidate the cognitive mechanisms underlying food choices, several variants of the multi-attribute drift diffusion model (DDM) were implemented <ref type="bibr">(25,</ref> <ref type="bibr">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The simplest model had five free parameters: starting bias (initial preference for eating the alternate item); non-decision time (NDT; part of trial in which the decision maker is not actively making a decision; includes time spent encoding choice options and making a motor response); decision boundary separation (bound sep; the amount of evidence required for a decision to be made); drift-rate for Healthiness (extent Healthiness influences choice; dH); and drift-rate for Tastiness (extent Tastiness influences choice; dT).
The basic model assumes individuals start to consider information about Tastiness and Healthiness of a given food choice at the same time (non-timevarying DDM).

We also considered time-varying DDMs that allow attributes to enter the choice process at different times (25, 27, 55), and those that included the accumulation of evidence for the Umami factor (Umami drift rate; dU). between the reference item-here trail mix, healthier but less tasty than the alternate item of donuts-and the alternate item.
text.formatted: We also considered time-varying DDMs that allow attributes to enter the choice process at different times <ref type="bibr">(25,</ref> <ref type="bibr">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55)</ref>, and those that included the accumulation of evidence for the Umami factor (Umami drift rate; dU). between the reference item-here trail mix, healthier but less tasty than the alternate item of donuts-and the alternate item.

text.text: In both cases, a relative value signal (RVS) begins with a value set by the bias (for alternate item) parameter (non-zero in these examples) and evolves with Gaussian noise, e, at every timepoint t (shown in segment and equation "A").

Once the Tastiness and Umami latency is reached (blue dotted line), the relative Tastiness and Umami values (difference in Tastiness and Umami between alternate and reference item), ΔT and ΔU, begin contributing to the RVS at a rate determined by its drift slopes dT (drift rate for Tastiness) and dU (drift rate for Umami).
This is depicted in segment and equation "B".

After the Healthiness attribute latency is reached (green dotted line), the relative Healthiness value (i.e., difference in Healthiness between alternate and reference item) ΔH, begins contributing to the RVS at a rate determined by its drift slope dH (drift rate for Healthiness).
This is depicted in segment and equation "C".
A decision is reached when the RVS becomes equal to or greater than the threshold for the reference or alternate items.

For Decision Maker 1, Healthiness enters the decision process at a similar time to Tastiness and Umami, which leads to an early contribution of the Healthiness attribute to the RVS, and selection of the subjectively healthy choice.
For Decision Maker 2, all parameters are the same except that the Healthiness attribute has a larger temporal delay (latency) in its effect on the drift rate.

Due to a later entry of Healthiness to the decision process, it begins contributing to the RVS later, and the alternate option boundary (for the tastier donuts) is crossed before the Healthiness attribute has a significant influence on choice.

text.text: Model fit was compared between models using five-fold cross-validation.
The model with highest accuracy was considered the best-fitting; relationships between parameters of this model and individual characteristics of interest were examined.
Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (56) was implemented as a secondary means of model comparison.

text.text: The role of self-control (Figure 8) Making healthy choices is often assumed to rely on "self-control", or choosing a healthier option, even over another option considered tastier.

text.text: Here, self-control was not frequently successfully implemented in general (approx. 25% of trials).

However, males (B = -0.01, [95% CI: -0.02, -0.00], p = 0.01), and those higher in Cognitive Restraint (B = 0.03, [95% CI: 0.02, 0.04], p < 0.001) successfully used self-control more frequently (see Table S8 for full model output).

text.text: The more frequent successful implementation of self-control by males seemingly contradicts the observation that they make fewer subjectively healthy choices.

However, self-control can only be implemented when conflicts between Healthiness and other concerns, such as Tastiness, arise, and males had more conflict trials (B = -0.85, [95% CI: -1.23, -0.46], p < 0.001; Fig. 8, top row), resulting in fewer healthy choices overall (see Fig. 7).

text.text: Multiple routes to subjectively healthier choices Fewer healthy choices can potentially emerge despite more frequent implementation of selfcontrol if a greater mismatch between tastiness and healthiness of foods creates more situations requiring such control (i.e., more conflict trials).

We explored this possibility by examining how selecting healthier options (proportion healthy choices) related to a) the association strength between Healthiness and Tastiness factors and b) self-control use.

Both Healthiness-Tastiness alignment (B = 0.07, [95% CI: 0.06, 0.07], p < 0.001) and self-control use (B = 0.07, [95% CI: 0.06, 0.07], p < 0.001; Fig 10) were associated with subjectively healthier choices (and when considering the objective healthiness criterion of low or high-fat foods; Supplementary Tables S12, S13) The correlation (Pearson's R) between Healthiness-Tastiness alignment and self-control use was 0.29, [95% CI: 0.23,0.34], p < 0.001], suggesting that some individuals may benefit from having both strategies available to them for healthier choices.

There was a quadratic effect for Umami, with more savory and sweeter foods rated higher in Tastiness (linear term: B = 0.15, [95% CI: 0.13, 0.17], p < 0.001; quadratic term: B = 0.14, [95% CI: 0.13, 0.16], p < 0.001; Supplementary Table S11).

text.text: Thus, when Umami was held constant, Tastiness was greater for the subjectively healthier food items (e.g., fruits over Skittles candies), whereas when Healthiness was held constant, Tastiness was greater for more savory foods, and for those foods with a stronger savory or sweet taste (e.g., pizza and doughnuts over wheat bread).

text.text: DDMs were applied to the data to parse and quantify distinct influences on choice, including the influence of different attributes on the accumulation of evidence, response bias, or response caution, and whether this varied across individual characteristics.
The best-fitting model (according to five-fold cross validation accuracy) included an influence of all three attributes (Tastiness, Healthiness, Umami) on drift rate, but not a latency parameter.
Thus, in this model all attributes were considered and began to influence evidence accumulation at the same time.

Associations of DDM-identified influences on evidence accumulation were largely consistent with the logistic models (Fig.

The pattern of results suggests that among individuals with higher levels of Cognitive Restraint, subjectively healthier choices may not result from careful deliberation but rather from attention towards food Healthiness combined with less deliberation when making choices.
This potentially allows subjectively healthier choices to be made with less effort and consideration.

The current study examined patterns of food choice in a large population cohort and characterized individual characteristics associated with variation in food choice and underlying cognitive processes.

By examining food decisions in relation to a large range of food attributes, we showed that three core dimensions of food-Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umamiinfluenced food preference significantly and, that the extent to which these factors influenced food preference varied across individuals.

Moreover, two distinct routes to making subjectively healthier food choices were identified: exertion of self-control when food Tastiness and Healthiness were in conflict and perceiving healthier foods as tastier.

Individual variation in the influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami attributes on food choices translated into differences in the extent to which individuals selected subjectively healthier food items.
The design of this study allowed for identifying multiple ways in which healthier choices could be achieved.
We assessed self-control use and alignment of Healthiness and Tastiness valuations as means of healthy choice, rather than focusing on one process in isolation.
The self-control process, which can only be observed when Healthiness and Tastiness valuations conflict, has received most attention (9, 16, 19, 25, 38).
text.formatted: The self-control process, which can only be observed when Healthiness and Tastiness valuations conflict, has received most attention <ref type="bibr">(9,</ref> <ref type="bibr">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38)</ref>.

text.text: However, by employing a range of foods representing a standard diet, rather than choosing among foods that were clearly "temptation" vs. "diet" foods, participant choices also involved foods that could be considered both healthy and tasty (or unhealthy and not tasty).

In addition, choices were made relative to a neutral food item (determined per individual), rather than pitting Healthiness and Tastiness against each other on every trial, and individuals' ratings of foods determined the number of health-taste conflicts and alignments.
Thus, it was possible to observe that both selfcontrol and aligning Tastiness and Healthiness were strongly associated with making healthier choices.
Implementation of these choice processes is thought to vary in the consideration and effort required.

Indeed, consistent with previous studies (21, 39), self-control implementation was associated with longer response times when successful, relative to trials in which self-control was not successfully implemented.
text.formatted: Indeed, consistent with previous studies <ref type="bibr">(21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39)</ref>, self-control implementation was associated with longer response times when successful, relative to trials in which self-control was not successfully implemented.

text.text: By contrast, considering healthier items to be tastier may represent a less effortful route towards healthier choices.
Notably, the application of these choice processes varied across individual characteristics.
Women, who showed a greater convergence of Tastiness and Healthiness valuations, but a decreased use of self-control, selected a greater number of healthier options relative to men.
That is, men, though using selfcontrol more successfully, made fewer healthy choices because they faced more conflict trials.

Thus, for women, despite choices being more strongly influenced by Tastiness, the alignment of Tastiness and Healthiness factors resulted in fewer conflict trials and less need for self-control to achieve healthier choices.

In a contrasting pattern, though self-control use did not differ as a function of BMI, individuals with higher BMI considered Healthiness less in choice, aligned Healthiness and Tastiness less, and made fewer healthy choices.
Individuals reporting greater levels of Cognitive Restraint were able to rely on both Healthiness-Tastiness alignment and greater self-control for healthier choices.

Greater convergence between Healthiness and Tastiness with higher Cognitive Restraint is consistent with a previous study observing this pattern in a small sample of female participants within a much lower BMI range (5).
In the present study, converging Healthiness and Tastiness resulted in less need for self-control, but we additionally observed that more restrained individuals used self-control more when needed.
Analyses of reaction time data indicated that the use of self-control may also be less effortful for these individuals.
Consistent with a prior study (5), individuals endorsing higher levels of restraint experienced a smaller decision-time cost when exerting self-control.
Outcomes of the DDM analyses also indicated that these individuals required less deliberation and choice preparation time to make decisions.
Overall, this decision process profile could suggest a more automatic choice pattern, or implementation of a rule.

Application of "if-then" rules (e.g., if I am hungry between meals, eat fruit) has been shown to be a powerful way to implement goals consistently (40) and may be one strategy underlying subjectively healthier choices by those who endorse Cognitive Restraint.
text.formatted: Application of "if-then" rules (e.g., if I am hungry between meals, eat fruit) has been shown to be a powerful way to implement goals consistently <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(40)</ref> and may be one strategy underlying subjectively healthier choices by those who endorse Cognitive Restraint.

text.text: Notably, Cognitive Restraint was not dispositive, but interacted with BMI, such that stronger Healthiness and weaker Tastiness effects on choice were most pronounced in those with lower BMIs.
This likely reflects that selfreported Cognitive Restraint, or intention to restrict, does not always translate into restricted food intake.
Collectively, the findings point toward multiple strategies for improving eating behavior, and that less effortful strategies can be applied to good effect.
One such strategy may be emphasizing the perceived tastiness of healthier food items.

Prior studies have demonstrated the potential for using taste-focused labelling to encourage selection of healthy foods, and have shown that this is more effective than health-focused labelling (41, 42).
text.formatted: Prior studies have demonstrated the potential for using taste-focused labelling to encourage selection of healthy foods, and have shown that this is more effective than health-focused labelling <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(41,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, increased exposure to healthier foods is likely critical for improving their palatability (43, 44), as more familiar foods are considered tastier and more liked (45).
text.formatted: Additionally, increased exposure to healthier foods is likely critical for improving their palatability <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44)</ref>, as more familiar foods are considered tastier and more liked <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(45)</ref>.

text.text: Reliance on less effortful strategies to guide eating behavior may be beneficial for health in general, but in the extreme may become maladaptive.
While the automatization of such strategies over time is the goal of interventions and nudges for healthier food choice, this could in some cases contribute to the maintenance of eating pathology.

Individuals with anorexia nervosa, a group with maladaptive levels of eating restraint, consistently report low-fat/calorie foods to be tastier than high-fat/calorie foods (21) (22) (23) and show a much higher likelihood of resisting tasty and unhealthy foods.
text.formatted: Individuals with anorexia nervosa, a group with maladaptive levels of eating restraint, consistently report low-fat/calorie foods to be tastier than high-fat/calorie foods <ref type="bibr">(21)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(23)</ref> and show a much higher likelihood of resisting tasty and unhealthy foods.

text.text: Automatization of these processes likely exacerbates the difficulties these individuals have increasing food intake (46) even when seeking treatment.
text.formatted: Automatization of these processes likely exacerbates the difficulties these individuals have increasing food intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(46)</ref> even when seeking treatment.

text.text: Whereas prior studies have tended to focus on subjective healthiness and tastiness (16, 17, 19, 21, 23-25, 27, 28, 47, 48), we considered the role of an additional latent dimension along which foods are characterized (4).

text.text: The Umami factor, capturing variability in protein, sodium and sugar content, as well as perceived sweetness/savoriness, also influenced food choices-albeit at a level akin to that of Healthiness rather than Tastiness (the strongest influence on choice).

Participants were significantly more likely to choose more savory rather than sweeter foods, consistent with studies showing that protein content is associated with food preferences in humans (32, 33).
text.formatted: Participants were significantly more likely to choose more savory rather than sweeter foods, consistent with studies showing that protein content is associated with food preferences in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we were able to examine the influence of the Umami factor in the context of the other main latent dimensions along which foods are considered and unpack its impact on decision mechanics.

Interestingly, females and individuals higher in Cognitive Restraint (who made healthier choices), were less inclined to find the sweetest and most savory foods (which were also rated as less healthy) tastier.
This suggests that accounting for the role of Umami in food choice allows a more complete characterization of dietary decision making and the strategies that support healthier choices.
Variation across age was not related to healthier choices, but distinct choice patterns emerged.

With increasing age, choices aligned more strongly with valuations of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami, potentially related to a slower decision process overall (as indicated by greater deliberation and choice preparation time in DDMs).

Interestingly, ratings of nutrient content were generally more strongly related to actual macronutrient content (Supplementary Table S17, Fig. S2) with increasing age, which may also reflect a more deliberate approach to evaluating food stimuli.
text.formatted: Interestingly, ratings of nutrient content were generally more strongly related to actual macronutrient content (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S17</ref>, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S2</ref>) with increasing age, which may also reflect a more deliberate approach to evaluating food stimuli.

text.text: Older individuals were distinguished by higher Tastiness ratings for more savory relative to sweeter foods (linear Umami effect).
These novel findings further emphasize the utility of assessing multiple factors conjointly when examining dietary decision making.

Changes in taste perception with aging (i.e., reduced sensitivity to salty, umami, bitter, sour, and sweet tastesthough particularly salty and bitter; (49, 50) could give rise to the observed changes in inputs to the decision process (i.e., estimated Tastiness, Umami) that combine with altered decision mechanics among older individuals.
text.formatted: Changes in taste perception with aging (i.e., reduced sensitivity to salty, umami, bitter, sour, and sweet tastesthough particularly salty and bitter; <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(49,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50)</ref> could give rise to the observed changes in inputs to the decision process (i.e., estimated Tastiness, Umami) that combine with altered decision mechanics among older individuals.

text.text: Interventions to change and maintain healthy eating as dietary requirements change with age likely need to consider these specific changes in valuation and choice processes.
This study has several strengths that contribute to advancing knowledge of food choice decision making.
The study population was large and diverse, representing a broad selection of age, weight, education, and geographical location, and was balanced on gender.

Food choice was modeled on the basis of recent data concerning the dimensions along which foods are evaluated (4), thereby presenting a more complete picture of the determinants of food choice than previous studies.

Results were robust to inclusion of potential confounders in statistical models, including adjustment for additional individual characteristics, and findings across the different analyses (e.g., mixed effects modelling of choice, RT, and outcomes of the DDMs) were consistent, supporting the reliability and validity of conclusions.
Nevertheless, the conclusions of the study should be considered in light of some limitations.
The data are cross-sectional and correlational, and longitudinal data will be needed to better understand precisely how food choices emerge and impact health.

Though the DDM selected for further analysis was the best performing amongst the models tested and the generating model was able to recapitulate the collected data, two of the model parameters did not recover well (particularly the parameter indexing the influence of Umami on choice; see Supplementary Material).
This may have been due to relatively small influence of Healthiness and Umami relative to Tastiness, which could complicate attempts to parse distinct effects on the drift rate (51).
text.formatted: This may have been due to relatively small influence of Healthiness and Umami relative to Tastiness, which could complicate attempts to parse distinct effects on the drift rate <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(51)</ref>.

text.text: Conclusions about the poorly recovered parameters, and their associations with individual characteristics, should therefore be made with caution.
We explored variation in food preferences across only a subset of individual characteristics.
We statistically adjusted for the role of income and education, however other factors (e.g., race, ethnicity) may have contributed to reported effects.
To enable further analyses and insights, the study data will be made freely available upon publication of this manuscript.
Finally, the study involved hypothetical choices rather than choices with real food outcomes.
However, prior studies suggest that similar decision processes are engaged during hypothetical versus real choice, and that hypothetical choices are predictive of actual choices (52).
text.formatted: However, prior studies suggest that similar decision processes are engaged during hypothetical versus real choice, and that hypothetical choices are predictive of actual choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(52)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, by collecting a range of ratings of food items and using food items carefully characterized in terms of macronutrient content, we could ascertain that individuals were fairly accurate in their perception of items and responded conscientiously.
Overall, the present study points to multiple approaches to making healthier choices, but that the use of these approaches varies across individuals.
Aligning Tastiness and Healthiness provides a low-effort route to healthy eating, as compared to self-control.
DDM evidence shows that these strategies manifest as distinct computational signatures, which vary systematically with individual characteristics.

Results confirm that subjective Tastiness is a predominant influence on choice and additionally show that an Umami factor contributes meaningfully to choice, at a level similar to the contribution of subjective Healthiness.

The role of Umami in food choice has been little studied to date, and the present findings highlight the importance of considering this characteristic in the design of mechanistic and intervention research, particularly among certain populations (e.g., older adults).
The findings highlight that healthier eating does not necessitate sacrificing tastiness and underscore the utility of identifying ways to improve the tastiness perceptions of healthier foods.
This and other strategies may circumvent the need for careful deliberation and self-control, which are prone to fail in inducing healthier choice, when deciding what to eat.
