Participants first rated their current hunger level, using a visual analogue scale that ranged from 0 to 10.
Next, they completed the food rating and choice tasks (described in the task section), followed by re-assessment of their hunger level.
Finally, assessments of self-reported eating behavior and psychopathology were completed and demographic information was collected.
At the end of the study, a debriefing page describing the study aims (stated as understanding normative ratings of food, estimates of nutrient content, and food choice) was displayed.

Food stimuli were 138 high-resolution color photographs of food items typical in a Western diet, including processed (e.g., pizza), unprocessed (e.g., cucumber sticks), sweet (e.g., brownie), savory (e.g., chicken fingers), single item (e.g., boiled eggs), item combinations (e.g., cereal with milk), snack foods (e.g., yogurt pretzels), and meals (e.g., rigatoni and sauce).
The stimulus set included food items with a mix of macronutrient content, ranging from low-to high-fat foods.
For categorical analyses, items were classified as low fat if < 30% calories came from fat, and high fat otherwise 4 .
text.formatted: For categorical analyses, items were classified as low fat if < 30% calories came from fat, and high fat otherwise 4 .

text.text: The stimulus set (Food Folio) is available to download with corresponding nutritional and normative rating information here: https://osf.io/483mx/.
text.formatted: The stimulus set (Food Folio) is available to download with corresponding nutritional and normative rating information here: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/483mx/">https://osf.io/483mx/</ref>.

text.text: Average ratings and characteristics of the stimulus set used have been reported elsewhere 1.
Each participant was presented with a 46-item subset of the total 138 foods, to limit testing sessions to approximately 1 hour.
One of 15 possible food-item subsets was randomly assigned to a participant.
Each subset included a similar selection and variety of foods, with high-fat foods constituting either 44% or 49% of all foods in each list.

Participants rated each item in their set along 17 separate attributes related to nutritional content (protein content, fat content, carbohydrate content, vitamin content, sodium content, sugar content, gluten content, caloric content) and subjective opinions (healthiness, tastiness, how tasty others think the food is, fillingness, savoriness, pleasantness of texture, disgustingness, feelings resulting from the food, and familiarity).

Participants rated all food items in their 46-item set consecutively on an attribute, using a slider scale displayed below the food item (see Figure 1; for the precise wording of the rating questions).
text.formatted: Participants rated all food items in their 46-item set consecutively on an attribute, using a slider scale displayed below the food item (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>; for the precise wording of the rating questions).

text.text: Scale responses were coded as numerical values from 0 to 10, with a resolution of 100 increments.

The order of rating each of the 17 attributes was randomized for each participant, food items were presented in a random order within each attribute rating section, and the direction of scale anchors was counterbalanced across participants (for details about the anchors, see the prior publication 1 ).
Each participant provided a total of 782 ratings (17 ratings for each of the foods in their 46-item set).

Choice Task After all ratings had been provided, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat "right now," between a reference food (randomly selected from items the participant had rated neutrally on both the tastiness and healthiness scale) and each of the other 45 foods in their specific stimulus set.

A neutral rating was taken as one in the middle of participants' own rating ranges (e.g., if a participant rated all foods between 4 and 8 for tastiness [on the 0-10 scale], a neutral tastiness rating would correspond to a value of 6).
When making their food choices, participants were asked to imagine snack-sized portions of the presented foods.

Preferences were indicated using a slider scale anchored by a strong preference for the reference food and a strong preference for the alternative food (corresponding to the numerical values of 0 and 10, respectively) (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Preferences were indicated using a slider scale anchored by a strong preference for the reference food and a strong preference for the alternative food (corresponding to the numerical values of 0 and 10, respectively) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants could not see the numeric values associated with slider position.

The Cognitive Restraint subscale of the TFEQ-18R, a reliable and validated 18-item assessment appropriate for use across non-clinical and clinical populations 5 , was used as a proxy for restrained eating behavior.
The TFEQ-18R additionally has the subscales Emotional Eating and Uncontrolled Eating and the full scale was administered.

Participants responded to each item on a four-point Likert-scale, using the options "definitely true", "mostly true", "mostly false", and "definitely false", scored numerically as 4, 3, 2, and 1, respectively.
The Cognitive Restraint subscale comprises six questions.
Responses to the questions are summed, such that higher scores are indicative of greater Cognitive Restraint.
The raw scale scores were standardized to a 0-100 scale using the formula: [(raw score-lowest possible raw score)/possible raw score range] ×100.
Cronbach's alpha was computed for each scale to determine internal reliability.
The overall reliability was good (Cronbach's alpha = 0.87).
The Cronbach's alpha for the Cognitive Restraint subscale was 0.80.
Participants' age, gender, education level, income, ethnicity, socio-economic status, region of the US, height, and weight were obtained by questionnaire at the end of the session.
Participant age was converted from categorical (18-25, 26-30, 31-35, 36-40, 41-45, 46-50, 51-55, 56-60, 61-65, 66-70, 71-75, and 76+, years) into numeric (coded 0 to 10).

Education was converted from the categorical variable into a numeric variable: "High school" and "Some college" coded as 0; "Associates degree" coded as 1; "Bachelors degree" code as 2; and "Masters degree", "Professional degree", or "Doctoral degree" coded as 3.
Income was converted from categorical ("Less than $20,000", "$20,000 to $34,999", "$35,000 to $49,999", "$50,000 to $74,999", "$75,000 to $99,999", and "Over $100,000") into numeric (0 to 5).
BMI was calculated using participants' self-reported height and weight.

As described previously 1 , an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) applied to the rating data indicated that the 17 ratings were best captured by three factors: a Tastiness factor capturing attributes such as texture and familiarity of foods in addition to how tasty a food was rated, a Healthiness factor capturing various macronutrient ratings in addition to caloric content, and an Umami factor capturing a savory/sweet dimension.
The Tastiness, Healthiness and Umami factors were largely uncorrelated: average Pearson's r values for correlations between these factors (for each participant) were < 0.06.
text.formatted: The Tastiness, Healthiness and Umami factors were largely uncorrelated: average Pearson's r values for correlations between these factors (for each participant) were < 0.06.

text.text: Capitalization of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami will be used to indicate referral to the composite variable.
For further details see 1.

Analyses focused on individual characteristics of interest (age, gender, BMI, and Cognitive Restraint), but all models additionally included Income and Education as covariates to account for these factors in analyses.

Correlations were calculated between numeric variables of interest as well as potential confounding variables: Pearson's correlation was applied when both variables were continuous; Spearman's correlation when one or both variables were ordinal (i.e., education, income).
T-tests (numeric outcomes) and Mann-Whitney U-tests (ordinal outcomes) were compared male and females across other characteristics.
Including hunger ratings obtained before and after the food rating and choice tasks as a covariate did not impact results, and hunger ratings were omitted from statistical models.

Analyses examining individual variability assessed whether data were best fit by the inclusion of an additional BMI*Cognitive Restraint interaction term (vs. main effects of BMI and Cognitive Restraint), given the potential for interactive effects of these factors on eating behavior 6-9 .
The interaction term was retained in analyses when significant and dropped otherwise.

Influence of Healthiness, Tastiness, and Umami on choice Continuous choice responses above and below 5 were recoded as 1 (choosing the trial-unique food) and 0 (not choosing the trial-unique food) respectively, as in previous studies of food choices 10-13 .
Choices that were exactly 5 were marked as missing (n = 199/47430 total responses; which constituted 0.4% of all responses).
To estimate the main effects of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors on choice across all participants, a logistic mixed effects regression was completed.

For the Umami factor, which differs from other factors in ranging from sweet to savory rather than from low to high in a clearly linear fashion, the possibility of a non-linear (quadratic) effect was assessed.
The inclusion of a quadratic Umami term improved model fit (chi-square = 15.49, p = 0.0168) and this term was added to the model.
The model included a random intercept for each participant and random intercepts for each food.
Random slopes were specified for Tastiness, Healthiness, Umami, and Umami 2 per participant, to allow for the differential effect of the three factors on choice across participants.
Fixed effects of Tastiness, Healthiness, Umami and Umami 2 were estimated.
Logistic mixed effects regression models probed how the influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami varied with individual characteristics.

In these models, binary choice ratings were regressed onto fixed effects of the interaction between each characteristic of interest (i.e., age, gender, BMI and cognitive restraint) and Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami.
All models specified random slopes for Healthiness, Tastiness, and Umami, per participant, and included a random intercept for each participant and food item:

To estimate the main effects of Healthiness and Umami on Tastiness across all participants, a linear mixed effects regression was completed, with Tastiness regressed onto the fixed effects Healthiness and Umami.
These models specified random slopes of Healthiness, Umami and Umami 2 per participant and random intercepts for each food.
Models assessing relationships between Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami improved with the addition of the quadratic Umami term (chi-square = 992.26, p < 0.001) and this term was retained.
text.formatted: Models assessing relationships between Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami improved with the addition of the quadratic Umami term (chi-square = 992.26, p < 0.001) and this term was retained.

text.text: To determine whether the association of Tastiness with Healthiness and Umami varied with individual characteristics, Tastiness scores were regressed onto interactions of each characteristic with Healthiness and Umami.
This model included random slopes of Healthiness and Umami per participant and random intercepts for each food.
The final model was thus:

To index the extent to which Healthiness and Tastiness were related (Healthiness-Tastiness alignment), the participant-specific effect (sum of fixed effect and random deviation for intercept and slope) of Healthiness was extracted for each participant.
Food items varied along a dimension from low to high fat, including intermediate items, and stimulus images were not explicitly labelled as low or high in fat.

Therefore, choice types were assessed relative to individual, subjective perceptions of Healthiness (i.e., whether individuals chose the perceived healthier or unhealthier of the reference food or the alternate food item before them).

The proportion of subjectively healthy choices was calculated as the proportion of trials in which the participant selected the item rated as healthier and multiple linear regression was used to estimate the association with each individual characteristic.

Self-control "Self-control" can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as those trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty (Healthiness rating above that of the reference item, and Tastiness rating below that of the reference item) or a food that was tasty and not healthy (Tastiness rating above that of the reference item, and Healthiness rating below that of the reference item).
The total number of conflict trials was counted for each participant.

Successful self-control trials were defined as conflict trials in which participants selected the healthy and not-tasty food or did not select the tasty and not-healthy food (i.e., opting for the reference item instead).

Self-control success was calculated for each participant by dividing the total number of successful self-control trials by the total number of conflict trials; multiple linear regression estimated the association wtih each individual characteristic of interest (total number of conflict trials was included as a covariate).

To examine how subjectively healthy choices related to self-control and Healthiness-Tastiness alignment, the proportion of subjectively healthy choices was regressed onto self-control success and health-taste alignment (extracted from the model estimating the Influence of Healthiness and Umami on Tastiness, described above) in a multiple linear regression model, including the number of conflict trials as a covariate.

To assess whether the use of self-control may be less effortful for certain individuals, mixed effects linear regression was used to estimate the difference in response time between successful and unsuccessful self-control trials.
These models included a random intercept for participant and a fixed effect of trial-type.
To further elucidate the cognitive mechanisms underlying food choices, several variants of the multi-attribute DDM were implemented 14-17 .

DDMs characterize choices as the result of a noisy evidence accumulation process in which evidence for a given choice option is repeatedly sampled over time, leading the decision maker to select or reject the option.
Implementation of the DDMs allows parsing of discrete but overlapping influences on choice to reveal the core mechanisms underlying choice behavior.

For example, distinct, latent mechanisms, such as speed of evidence accumulation, degree of response caution, or the timing at which information begins to be sampled, may affect behavior similarly but are distinct decision mechanisms.

In the multi-attribute extension of the DDM 14,15,17,18 evidence for distinct attributes (e.g., Tastiness, Healthiness) is sampled at each point in time, allowing for estimation of the unique contribution of these attributes to choice, while also accounting for other decision processes (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: In the multi-attribute extension of the DDM 14,15,17,18 evidence for distinct attributes (e.g., Tastiness, Healthiness) is sampled at each point in time, allowing for estimation of the unique contribution of these attributes to choice, while also accounting for other decision processes (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Several models were fit to the reaction time and choice data.

In the simplest model there were five free parameters: starting bias (initial preference for eating the alternate item); non-decision time (NDT; part of the trial in which the decision maker is not actively making a decision; this parameter includes the time spent encoding choice options and making a motor response); decision boundary separation (bound sep; the amount of evidence required for a decision to be made); drift-rate for Healthiness (extent to which Healthiness influences choice); and drift-rate for Tastiness (extent to which Tastiness influences choice).
Greater drift rates are thought to reflect more goal-directed choices, whereas choice biases can indicate automated selection processes 19-21.
The basic model assumes that individuals start to consider information about the Tastiness and Healthiness of a given food choice at the same time (non-time-varying DDM).

To account for a temporally dynamic choice process, we additionally considered time-varying DDMs that allow attributes to enter the choice process at different times, such that the attributes have separate drift latencies 14,17,22 .

Drift latencies causally affect choice outcomes 23 , and not accounting for the different drift latencies across the distinct attributes (where they exist) may lead to erroneous inferences (e.g., slower latency of an attribute is interpreted as lower drift weighting 17,22 .

We also assessed the fit of models that modelled the accumulation of evidence for the Umami factor (Umami drift rate), in addition to drift rates for Healthiness and Tastiness, and models in which the latency of Umami, Healthiness and Tastiness differed, yielding the following models: 1: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT 2: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT + dU 3: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT, latency H (relative to latency T) 4: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT + dU, latency U (relative to latency H + latency T) 5: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT + dU, latency H (relative to latency U + latency T) 6: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT + dU, latency T (relative to latency U + latency H) DDM analyses included trials in which a clear preference for the reference or the alternate food was indicated (i.e., only trials in which choice responses were >= 6 or =< 4).
text.formatted: We also assessed the fit of models that modelled the accumulation of evidence for the Umami factor (Umami drift rate), in addition to drift rates for Healthiness and Tastiness, and models in which the latency of Umami, Healthiness and Tastiness differed, yielding the following models: 1: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT 2: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT + dU 3: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT, latency H (relative to latency T) 4: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT + dU, latency U (relative to latency H + latency T) 5: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT + dU, latency H (relative to latency U + latency T) 6: bias, NDT, bound sep, dH + dT + dU, latency T (relative to latency U + latency H) DDM analyses included trials in which a clear preference for the reference or the alternate food was indicated (i.e., only trials in which choice responses were >= 6 or =< 4).

text.text: Only participants with at least 35 trials were included to maximize the stability and accuracy of parameter estimates 24 , resulting in a final sample of 705 participants for the DDM analyses.
All models were fit using hierarchical Bayesian parameter estimation with JAGS, and implemented with the runjags package in R. DDM model selection.
To determine the best fitting model, a five-fold cross-validation approach was adopted.
This allowed for examining model fit while retaining the hierarchical structure of the data.

Model accuracy was calculated by fitting the model to 4/5 folds of data (each fold included 4/5 of data from each participant), and sampling 1000 samples from the posterior to generate 1000 sets of parameter values.

These parameter sets were used alongside the empirical rating data to simulate, for each individual and for each left-out trial (i.e., in the 1/5 of data not used to fit the model), 1000 data points denoting RT and choice.
The rate of error for each binary choice was averaged across simulations and trials, and folds, for each individual.
The mean error rate was then calculated in the full sample.

While cross-validated error rate was the primary mean of model comparison, models were also compared with the Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation 25  (PSIS-LOO) statistic, computed on the systematically thinned 3000-draw posterior.
PSIS-LOO re-weights the posterior draws to approximate the posterior that would have been obtained without each trial and evaluates that trial's predictive density under it.
For some trials the importance weights are heavy-tailed (Pareto k > 0.7), indicating that this approximation is unreliable.
text.formatted: For some trials the importance weights are heavy-tailed (Pareto k > 0.7), indicating that this approximation is unreliable.

text.text: To examine whether such trials influenced the conclusions, all trials with k > 0.7 in any model were removed and PSIS-LOO for all models on the remaining common subset was calculated in sensitivity analyses (note that the removal of these trials did not affect inferences concerning the best fitting model).
text.formatted: To examine whether such trials influenced the conclusions, all trials with k > 0.7 in any model were removed and PSIS-LOO for all models on the remaining common subset was calculated in sensitivity analyses (note that the removal of these trials did not affect inferences concerning the best fitting model).

text.text: Inputs to PSIS-LOO typically comprise the pointwise log-likelihood reported by JAGS.
However, this quantity is conditional on the trial-level drift rate, a latent parameter informed only by that trial's response.
Conditioning on it therefore does not constitute an out-of-sample predictive density.

Consequently, the marginal pointwise likelihood was computed, integrating over the trial-level drift: p(yᵢ | θ) = ∫ f(yᵢ | a, τ, β, w) • N(w | ℓî, σ) dw where a, τ and β are the participant's boundary separation, non-decision time and starting-point bias, ℓî is the model-implied drift for trial i, and σ the participant-level drift standard deviation.
The resulting density depends only on participant-level parameters and the trial's known attribute values and is therefore a valid input to PSIS-LOO.

The integral was computed for each of 3000 draws from the posterior and evaluated by 25-node Gauss-Hermite quadrature, with the Wiener first-passage density implemented following Navarro and Fuss (2009) 26.
For the best fitting model, the model was refit using all data.
The posterior was systematically thinned from 30000 to 3000 samples.

The 3-independent chains (1000 samples each) were visually examined for convergence, and the split R-hat statistic 25 was computed, for each of the population parameters (i.e., the mean model-estimated values across participants) in the hierarchical model.
The R-hat statistic is a key indicator of model convergence and was calculated as the square-root of the ratio of the between-chain variance:within-chain variance.
Values < 1.03 are considered acceptable.
text.formatted: Values < 1.03 are considered acceptable.

text.text: A parameter recovery exercise was also undertaken.

Here, the mean parameter value for each individual (from the best-fitting model) was used in combination with trial-wise Healthiness, Tastiness and Umami values to simulate trial data for each participant.
The model was then fit to the simulated RT and choice data and Pearson's correlations between the generative and derived parameters were estimated.

Posterior predictive checks were performed making 1000 draws of parameter values from the thinned posterior parameter distribution, using these parameters to simulate new data (n=1000 datasets), and examining whether empirical means fell within the 95% HDI of the simulated RT data (Figure S3).
text.formatted: Posterior predictive checks were performed making 1000 draws of parameter values from the thinned posterior parameter distribution, using these parameters to simulate new data (n=1000 datasets), and examining whether empirical means fell within the 95% HDI of the simulated RT data (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_16">S3</ref>).

text.text: To examine whether the simulated data from the best-performing model was able to recapitulate patterns in the collected data, the similarity of RT distributions for trials in which the alternate item was chosen or rejected was examined visually.
RT distributions were separated by high and low (per median split for each individual) values of each attribute.
Plots and statistics (i.e., R-hat 27 ) indicated convergence of estimates for the parameters of the best-fitting DDM model.
Parameter recovery was good to excellent for most of the model parameters, but poor for the Umami term (i.e., Pearson's correlation = 0.36).
Distributions of data generated from the best-fitting model were similar to those for collected data (Figures S4 and S5).
text.formatted: Distributions of data generated from the best-fitting model were similar to those for collected data (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_17">S4</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_18">S5</ref>).

text.text: Data were excluded from analyses for participants whose self-reported height and weight values led to uninterpretable BMIs (e.g., negative values; n = 43).
In addition, given the low prevalence of BMIs outside of the 18.5-60 kg/m2 range 2,3 , individuals with a BMI outside that range (n=40) were excluded from analyses to promote generalizability.

An additional exclusion criterion for this study was missing data for variables of interest (age, gender, Cognitive Restraint, and BMI) or possible confounders (income, education); n = 2, resulting in a final sample size of 1052.
Thought for food: Individual differences in how food decisions are made

Participants were individuals who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study between July 2018 and August 2019 1 , recruited using a convenience sampling strategy, and paid $7.25 for study completion.
Participation was open to those aged 18 years or older and residing in the United States; there were no other exclusion criteria.
A total of 1,137 individuals participated.
Prior to beginning the study, participants viewed a consent form that described the study procedures, efforts to ensure confidentiality, and participation compensation.
Participants provided informed consent by clicking an icon to continue with the experiment.

Figure1.
Study overview.

Participants completed ratings of images of food on 17 different attributes, prior to completing a Food Choice phase in which they indicated whether they preferred a food that varied, displayed on the right, or a constant Reference food, displayed on the left.
The Reference food was selected per individual to be neutral per their ratings of Tastiness and Healthiness.
A factor analysis of ratings yielded three central dimensions, subsequently used to examine food choices and their variation with individual characteristics.
The Tastiness factor captured texture and familiarity, in addition to how tasty a food was rated.
The Healthiness factor captured ratings across various macronutrients in addition to caloric content.
The Umami factor captured a savory/sweet dimension including protein and how filling a food was reported to be.
Figure 2.
Examples of the decision process in the three-attribute time-varying Drift Diffusion Model.

Two hypothetical decision makers (Decision Maker 1, left panel, and Decision Maker 2, right panel) selectbetween the reference item-here trail mix, healthier but less tasty than the alternate item of donuts-and the alternate item.

In both cases, a relative value signal (RVS) begins with a value set by the bias (for alternate item) parameter (non-zero in these examples) and evolves with Gaussian noise, e, at every timepoint t (shown in segment and equation "A").

Once the Tastiness and Umami latency is reached (blue dotted line), the relative Tastiness and Umami values (difference in Tastiness and Umami between alternate and reference item), ΔT and ΔU, begin contributing to the RVS at a rate determined by its drift slopes dT (drift rate for Tastiness) and dU (drift rate for Umami).
This is depicted in segment and equation "B".

After the Healthiness attribute latency is reached (green dotted line), the relative Healthiness value (i.e., difference in Healthiness between alternate and reference item) ΔH, begins contributing to the RVS at a rate determined by its drift slope dH (drift rate for Healthiness).
This is depicted in segment and equation "C".
A decision is reached when the RVS becomes equal to or greater than the threshold for the reference or alternate items.

For Decision Maker 1, Healthiness enters the decision process at a similar time to Tastiness and Umami, which leads to an early contribution of the Healthiness attribute to the RVS, and selection of the subjectively healthy choice.
For Decision Maker 2, all parameters are the same except that the Healthiness attribute has a larger temporal delay (latency) in its effect on the drift rate.

Due to a later entry of Healthiness to the decision process, it begins contributing to the RVS later, and the alternate option boundary (for the tastier donuts) is crossed before the Healthiness attribute has a significant influence on choice.
Figure adapted from(27).
Figure 3.
Influence of food attribute factors on choice.
Associations between average Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factor scores and choices across foods are displayed.
All three factors significantly influenced the choice of foods, with the strongest association for the Tastiness factor.
